adventure.title: The Witch of Blackbriar Hall
adventure.synopsis: Blackbriar Vale remembers Judith Crowl by what arrived when no one else would send it: grain during the famine, beds during the pox, burial money when a household could not pay. Fifteen years later, each kindness has a receipt. Judith selects the vale's witches, removes their children, stores inconvenient dead, and keeps every household close enough to answer her knock. She bought that power through three chosen betrayals: nineteen refugees barred inside a burning granary for the Guest in Ash, thirty-one plague dead erased in quicklime for the Worm in White, and stolen children's names lowered into Moonless Mere for the Child Behind Glass. Canon Ysra's examiners were already approaching when Mara Sedge linked seven false prosecutions and Nell Sedge mapped the mirror dormitory. Judith took Nell, moved Mara's burning before the customary answer-night, and turned the annual Renewal of Mercy into the Hollow Feast. At first light she places the torch in eleven-year-old Tomas Sedge's hands. By midnight, the Mercy Book, household carriers, and four controlled living voices can join every door still answering Judith's claim. The commissioned company must keep the Sedge family alive, find the people and records Judith has moved, expose the roads behind her apparent omniscience, complete the material obligations she inverted, and break a feast built to continue after its hostess dies.
adventure.premise: Canon Ysra Vale sent your company to compare burial fees with parish graves and inspect Saint Mercy House after two letters went unanswered. Before dawn, Brother Caldus's rider finds you on the road with a sharper report: Nell Sedge vanished three nights ago, Mara Sedge named Judith Crowl as the taker, and the reeve has advanced Mara's execution before the customary answer-night. You reach Saint Orra's Gallows as Judith orders Mara's eleven-year-old son to light the pyre. The death roll has been cut and rebound. The reeve hides a blackthorn token. Every household owes Judith a sack, cure, bed, burial, or life. Canon Ysra's seal can hold Mara alive, preserve evidence, and protect immediate witnesses; it cannot govern the vale for you. The Renewal of Mercy begins before dusk. At midnight Judith means to turn the vale's separate debts into the Unwelcome Court's common invitation.
adventure.explanation:
Judith Crowl is the witch. Fifteen years ago she sought the Unwelcome Court because affection could be withdrawn, while debt could be recorded, inherited, and enforced. She chose each bargain, renewed it when it weakened, and built ordinary relief work around the access it purchased.

The Guest in Ash was her first account. During the famine, Judith entered nineteen road families on Saint Vey's refuge roll, took their labor on the granary roof, barred the doors on the third night, and welcomed the Guest across the threshold they trusted. The fire burned inward. The Guest now carries her across marked hearths, turns domestic flame against a household, closes claimed exits, and folds passage into soot. Her private ledger still records all nineteen as safely discharged.

The Worm in White followed during the pox. Families paid Judith to carry thirty-one bodies to honest ground. She cut off the tags, laid the dead in quicklime beneath the orchard, and denied each body a final witness. The Worm moves sickness, works abandoned flesh, spoils stores, and lays Judith's wounds on the unburied. Later patients whose suffering inconvenienced her accounts became renewal bodies.

The Child Behind Glass came with Saint Mercy House. Judith records children under their whole names, copies chosen names onto silvered slips, and lowers the vessels into Moonless Mere. The Child lends voices, dreams, false recognition, written command, and reflected roads. It named the price before Judith paid it; she returned with more names and built forms, dormitories, transfers, and receiving beds into a steady acquisition system. Saint Mercy House is not an independent good she later corrupted. Judith made the care effective because every cured fever, occupied bed, and winter meal placed another person inside a room, record, or obligation she could inventory.

Judith also manufactures the witches she condemns. Petition paper becomes a planted poppet. An illness moves into a household. The dependent most likely to be believed disappears. Ordinary officers receive enough fear or favor to finish the accusation, and Judith offers the survivors grain, medicine, custody, or protection. Tokens, receipts, copied names, and stolen hearth ash extend a network that crows, servants, mirrors, wagons, and marked people must physically carry. Her knowledge is formidable because the network is busy, finite, and well supplied.

That distributed system kept any one failure from exposing the whole. It also ended when Caldus's duplicate burial figures reached Canon Ysra, Mara connected seven prosecutions, and Nell mapped the mirror dormitory. Judith's couriers learned when the examiners would arrive. She took Nell, framed Mara, advanced the burning, and rewrote the Renewal of Mercy as a final consolidation. Slow ownership is about to become public evidence.

Forty-seven households display a blackthorn token. Eleven more have signed the Mercy Book. Five have done neither. Judith means the reeve's Renewal oath to answer for the vale and catch the unmarked doors, but an explicit household refusal blocks a new connection and can turn an existing copied door outward once its material carriers are revoked. The Mercy Book names hosts. Tokens and stolen ash carry household claims. Seven silvered names prepare the choir bays and coordinate the Glass Nurse, but a vessel is not a voice: at least four living, controlled speakers must stand in the Underhall. The Hollow Feast operates while any two of three components—the Mercy Book, token network, and captive choir—remain joined. Midnight reaches only the doors still connected.

Ysra's writ authorizes record inspection, evidence preservation, a temporary stay of an unlawful execution, and immediate witness protection. It grants no permanent rule, general command over the reeve's guards, title to Blackbriar property, or power to dispose of victims without their families and witnesses. Later operations rest on discovered unlawful custody, immediate rescue, ordinary defense, willing household or parish cooperation, and narrow public orders from local officers who accept responsibility. Government, property settlement, and final judgment wait for outside civil and chapel authorities.

Each pact ends only when living people complete the obligation Judith inverted. Open the Burned Refuge without welcoming the Guest, restore the nineteen names, and burn the lying shelter ledger in a hearth freely offered by someone Judith betrayed. Identify the pit-dead, lift them safely from quicklime, and give them burial or burning beneath a bell that states where they were found and who denied them. Speak each stolen name back in an unborrowed reflection before breaking its vessel. Doors, records, bodies, witnesses, transport, care, and final disposition are the rite.

Two severed pacts make Judith's body mortal. Three prevent the Court from taking up her claim cleanly. Killing her may be necessary, but the common welcome can outlive her through the Mercy Book, household tokens, and captive choir. Removing any two components collapses the valley-wide claim. Unrevoked household carriers may still support smaller claims afterward.

Keep Judith in the work. At the gallows she makes Tomas hold the torch. At Saint Mercy House she names the meals, medicines, bottles, and receiving beds a rescue will require. At Blackbriar Hall she offers exact benefits whose costs she has assigned to someone else. Retaliation strikes a person the company promised to protect and arrives as an accounting correction. Judith remembers debts perfectly and wrongdoing only when it belongs to another person.

Her voice stays controlled and domestic. Captives are residents, commands are placements, stolen property is relief stock, and coercion is the part of mercy that sentimental people refuse to name. She uses names as receipts: ‘Ansel whom I restored,’ ‘Caldus whose sister I housed,’ ‘Tomas whom I am still willing to forgive.’ Her claim is not innocence. It is that everyone else lacks the nerve to choose who pays. The relief remains real because false usefulness would bind no one.

The clue distribution follows the work. Public machinery leaves many witnesses; exact severance procedures survive in fewer hands and places. Every clue should come from a household, record, victim, route, tool, patron, or worker able to know it. The finale supplies no compensating manual for discoveries missed elsewhere.

Judith has one body and bounded information. Track where she goes after the gallows. Roads, valid Guest crossings, and complete reflected routes can move her. Crows, borrowed voices, commanded guards, hearthlings, the Glass Nurse, and patron manifestations carry intention without duplicating her. Between substantial company operations, spend at most one major response through one surviving channel and leave its receipt: soot, paper, silver scoring, a returning symptom, a courier, a moved wagon, or a witnessed handoff.

The opening begins shortly after dawn, and midnight is a working deadline. One company cannot personally complete ten large operations in sequence. Once procedure, materials, witnesses, care, and authority are established, named local crews may continue persistent work while the company moves to the next critical decision. Record who was entrusted, what remains incomplete, and which routes carry reports. Parallel labor never becomes automatic success, and travel never empties an encounter offstage. At midnight, advance the Underhall to the components actually assembled.

Keep knowledge, access, readiness, care, pact work, feast machinery, and Judith's control separate. Copied evidence remains copied. An opened door remains open. A body honestly buried does not return to the Worm. A restored name stays restored. Direct assault can win rescues, records, routes, or component losses early; it cannot perform a remote severance or conjure the people and materials that work requires.

references.title: Judith Crowl
references.summary: Blackbriar Vale's relief patron and deliberate witch, who turns real aid into inherited debt through three chosen betrayals and a finite network of hearths, names, records, servants, and roads.
references.content:
## Mercy entered in her own hand

Judith Crowl found grain during famine, beds during pox, and burial money when other authorities would not advance them. The help was real. Judith's fraud lies in the title she claims afterward: a meal becomes entry, a cure becomes custody, a bed becomes a name in her keeping, and gratitude becomes an obligation descendants may inherit. She speaks at household volume and uses debts as surnames because she wants coercion to sound like an account everyone already accepted.

## Three guests deliberately welcomed

Judith chose the Unwelcome Court rather than stumbling into it. She barred nineteen promised refugees inside a burning granary for the Guest in Ash, erased thirty-one plague dead in quicklime for the Worm in White, and surrendered children's written names through Moonless Mere for the Child Behind Glass. She renewed each bargain when it weakened and built ordinary relief institutions around the access each patron purchased. The care does not excuse the machinery; it is part of the machinery.

## A busy network is not omniscience

Judith learns and acts through physical carriers: marked hearths, stolen ash, blackthorn tokens, signed pages, written names, crows, servants, wagons, bottles, mirrors, and willing collaborators. She cannot read an unspoken plan, see through an isolated token, or move a person without a surviving road or channel. Exposing one carrier narrows her reach without erasing the others. Her bodily location, injuries, custody, surrender, retaliation, active patron channels, and final disposition belong to the adventure state actually reached.

references.title: Canon Ysra Vale
references.summary: The canon whose burial discrepancies and unanswered Mercy House letters produced a narrow inspection commission able to preserve evidence and witnesses without governing Blackbriar Vale.
references.content:
## A commission sent before the pyre

Canon Ysra Vale acted before Mara Sedge was accused. Duplicate burial fees, missing graves, and two unanswered letters from Saint Mercy House were enough for her to send examiners into Blackbriar Vale. Brother Caldus's later addendum sharpened the emergency; it did not create the original inquiry. That chronology matters whenever Judith claims the commission was invented to rescue one favored prisoner.

## What the seal can hold

Ysra's writ authorizes inspection of parish and charitable records, preservation of evidence, protection of named witnesses, and a temporary stay while a defective capital charge is reviewed. It does not dismiss the reeve, command every guard, open every private room, transfer custody of every child, seize Judith's stores, or make the commissioned company the vale's government. New authority requires a new basis: an unlawful detention, a household's invitation, a public local order, chapel witness, or ordinary defense against violence.

## Law must be received somewhere

A seal can demand a docket; it cannot carry a patient, guard a threshold, copy a ledger, feed a household, or make a frightened official obey. Ysra's authority is strongest when local people accept bounded responsibility for those acts and weakest when outsiders treat the writ as a substitute for consent or care. The commission's bearer, recognition, exercised scope, orders, and legal effect remain matters of play.

references.title: Brother Caldus Merrow
references.summary: Blackbriar parish clerk, compromised burial witness, and keeper of the dates, inks, fees, and chapel fragments that turn missing bodies into a provable institutional pattern.
references.content:
## The clerk who counted absent bodies

Brother Caldus Merrow remembers a missing page by its date, ink, fee, and place in the parish sequence. Burial payments arrived for bodies that never reached parish ground. Later leaves were substituted, the Chapel of the Free Witness was closed under the wrong ordinance, and records that should have met were kept apart. His first addendum put those discrepancies beside Nell Sedge's disappearance and Mara's accelerated sentence.

## Concealment under threat

Judith threatened Caldus's widowed sister Adela and her son Lark until he hid discrepancies and falsified later records. That coercion explains his silence; it does not make the altered pages true or erase his responsibility for helping conceal them. Caldus can identify the false famine ordinance, locate burial fragments, explain the closure chronology, and distinguish an original parish hand from a substituted leaf.

## A witness, not a complete ritual book

Caldus knows where the chapel's threshold, burial, and naming offices were divided, but he does not carry every rite from memory. The honest bell and counter-rites require surviving texts, material repair, and free witnesses rather than clerical rank alone. His cooperation, protection, record custody, route, testimony, and family safety must be established in play rather than supplied by this record.

references.title: Mara Sedge
references.summary: A Blackbriar midwife whose exact birth and illness records expose the repeated structure behind seven prosecutions, and whose practical law begins with keeping named children alive.
references.content:
## Names, hours, complications

Mara Sedge is thirty-eight and records births by mother, witness, hour, and complication because memory becomes generous after danger passes. She applies the same discipline to illness, cures, custody, gifts, and accusations. Her children are Nell, thirteen; Tomas, eleven; and Pate, seven. She refuses any account that turns one of them into a symbol before naming where that child will sleep and who will answer for the door.

## Seven prosecutions laid side by side

Mara compared seven cases by household rather than theory: a Judith gift, a convenient symptom or planted object, a missing dependent or body, an officer's altered story, and property or custody moving toward Blackbriar. Red thread marks dates; birthing blue marks names. The packets do not prove that every case used the same magic. They prove that Judith repeatedly joined magic to ordinary offices, frightened witnesses, and beneficiaries who preferred not to ask what paid for their relief.

## Refusal has a material form

Mara understands the household rule Judith suppresses: accepting aid grants no permanent entry. A resident may name the gift, withdraw access to their own name, room, bed, threshold, or hearth, and remove or cover the physical carrier. Mara's execution clock, stay, custody, injuries, testimony, standing, children, and household outcome remain live. Her record preserves the woman capable of recognizing the pattern, not the result of her attempt to expose it.

references.title: Nell Sedge
aliases: Nell Sedge of the mirror dormitory
references.summary: Mara Sedge's thirteen-year-old daughter, an observant captive cartographer who counted the mirror dormitory, named seven linked children, and learned the safe order for returning a stolen name.
references.content:
## A map scratched where adults would not look

Nell Sedge is thirteen. She drew a long house, hanging mirrors, and crows flying toward a wood where the sun appeared in the wrong place, then hid the map beneath her bed. She also listed seven children who sometimes answered in voices not their own: Nell, Amey Fen, Jo Rusk, Lark Merrow, Perrin Mett, Sella Darr, and Corin Pike. The list establishes a shared naming system without pretending all seven bodies or vessels occupy one room.

## Count the mirrors before breaking one

At Saint Mercy House, Nell counted every mirror, found the sealed east stair, and learned where the iron key could be hidden. She witnessed failed attempts to free stolen names and knows the necessary order: establish identity through the owner or a free witness, recover an unborrowed reflection, speak the name back, wait for the reflection to belong to the person, and only then break the vessel. Violence against the glass before that sequence harms the owner rather than defeating Judith cleanly.

## A child with evidence, not an evidence object

Nell knows other children, rooms, voices, and routes because she watched and remembered. Her knowledge does not authorize adults to move her body, speak for her, or decide that a rescued name is the same as a rescued child. Her location, custody, bodily safety, testimony, name-vessel condition, consent, healing, and final guardianship remain live adventure state.

references.title: Tomas Sedge
aliases: Tomas Sedge of the gallows green
references.summary: Mara Sedge's eleven-year-old son, a direct witness to Judith's public coercion who knows Nell's hiding places and Quill's route and responds to concrete protection rather than adult moral summaries.
references.content:
## The child Judith asks to carry the sentence

Tomas Sedge is eleven. Judith's method at Saint Orra's Gallows is to place the torch in his hands, threaten his siblings, and call whatever follows a son's consent. Tomas therefore understands one part of Judith's rule with unusual clarity: an adult can manufacture obedience by making a child responsible for the harm done to the people he loves.

## Plain questions before brave plans

Tomas wants to know whether Mara can breathe, where Pate will sleep, who will stop Captain Cleft, and what happens if a promised refuge fails. He has no patience for adults discussing him as cargo or praising his courage while leaving the immediate danger intact. Give him one credible action and a named adult responsibility, and he acts quickly.

## What he noticed at the croft

Tomas knows where Nell hid drawings, which crow watched the chimney, and how Quill approached the Sedge hearth. He is also a public witness to the terms Judith offered and the officers who helped stage them. None of that makes his testimony automatically safe, believed, or available. His torch, location, custody, willingness to speak, immediate safety, and family outcome remain decisions and consequences of play.

references.title: Reeve Ansel Pell
references.summary: Blackbriar Vale's frightened civil magistrate, cured through another man's suffering and practiced at hiding his own false seizures inside passive grammar and borrowed ordinances.
references.content:
## The reeve whom Judith restored

Ansel Pell suffered a wasting sickness until Judith moved it into Elian Darr. Pell lived, Darr was accused of blighting him, and Blackbriar Hall received the Darr lease after conviction. Pell later signed false seizures and emergency charges while telling himself that the documents arrived already decided. He speaks in passive grammar: a charge “was brought,” an ordinance “was found,” a child “has been asked.”

## Civil power with a narrow honest use

The reeve's office can recognize a lawful stay, demand a docket, preserve evidence, release or reassign guards, authorize a bounded evacuation, and place local acts on a public record. It cannot make a grain ordinance govern witchcraft, turn Judith's accusations into sworn testimony, or grant one household's consent on behalf of another. Pell knows more of that boundary than his conduct admits.

## Fear is an explanation, not an acquittal

Judith can threaten Pell through the cure receipt, stolen hearth ash, and the sickness she once displaced. He wants a lawful reason to stop and someone else to bear the cost of stopping. Whether he retains office, cooperates, confesses, falls ill, issues a useful order, enters custody, or resumes collaboration remains live. The stable fact is the compromised magistrate and the authority he repeatedly misused.

references.title: Beadle Odo Vane
references.summary: A willing court collaborator who turns Judith's injuries into charges, custody, and household obligations, and whose love of office survives exposure more readily than his loyalty to any person.
references.content:
## Injury made procedural

Beadle Odo Vane drafts charges, cites ordinances, prepares seizures, keeps seals, and supplies the phrases by which coercion becomes an official act. He knew the famine ordinance did not authorize Mara Sedge's execution. He has repeatedly chosen substitution over error: accused for person, dependent for child, disposition for murder, beneficiary for household under threat.

## The daughter whose place excuses everyone else

Odo's daughter received a place through Saint Mercy House. He treats preservation of that advantage as permission to ruin other families, close the chapel, falsify custody, and join Judith's household account. The motive is intimate; the collaboration is willing. Exposure may make him bargain over a record or captive, but it does not reliably make him repent.

## A seal is not the law it imitates

Odo can control access to records, lecterns, ink, prepared charges, and the mechanics of a public reading. He cannot create lawful authority by quoting an unrelated ordinance or make a household welcome Judith by naming it from a page. Separate him from ink, knife, seal, and prepared text when his procedural skill matters. His allegiance, control, movement, survival, bargains, and use of the Mercy Book remain live adventure state.

references.title: Captain Varro Cleft
references.summary: Judith's Blackthorn commander, a willing enforcer who turns official language into permission for violence and manages guards, prisoners, coerced testimony, and the roads connecting accusation to disappearance.
references.content:
## Violence waiting for a lawful phrase

Captain Varro Cleft speaks in distances and commands. He enjoys the moment when an ordinance, custody paper, or frightened official gives him permission to hurt someone while calling the harm procedure. He stages arrests, transports prisoners, compels testimony through threatened dependents, and keeps violence moving after Judith has left the room.

## A command company, not one enchanted body

Cleft's Blackthorn force includes marked guards whose written names, tokens, or cure receipts can seize bodily control and ordinary paid guards who remain capable of refusal. Command shows itself: a mark heats, a jaw locks, eyes gray, or a voice changes before movement. The distinction matters. Magic may explain one act without excusing Cleft's chosen cruelty or making every guard equally bound.

## Roads are part of the office

Cleft's reach depends on guards, wagons, custody papers, crow messages, and people willing to receive an order. Remove command, isolate him from the company, protect the threatened dependent, or make a lawful refusal public, and the violence becomes harder to disguise and execute. His present allegiance, force, location, captives, coercive bargains, survival, and control of any route remain live.

references.title: Sister Harl
aliases: Sister Harl of Saint Mercy House
references.summary: The steward of Saint Mercy House, culpable for hidden naming and coercive transfers yet competent at keeping a real institution alive, and most vulnerable when Judith treats residents as expendable feast material.
references.content:
## Care kept by ownership

Sister Harl administers Saint Mercy House. She knows its intake forms, beds, kitchens, infirmary, resident needs, name repetitions, punishment routines, and transfer routes. The house feeds children and treats patients because Harl can organize people and stores. She also collects names, orders coercive discipline, conceals rooms, and accepts custody as leverage over families.

## The institution before the resident

Harl believes dependency should be used without apology. She has told herself that Judith preserves Saint Mercy House and that hidden naming is the price of keeping it open. Evidence of abuse alone makes her defend the institution more fiercely. Proof that Judith intends to spend residents rather than preserve them can break that argument only when paired with a credible plan for beds, food, medicines, carriers, receiving households, and immediate safety.

## Competence does not settle loyalty

Harl can identify residents, medical burdens, bottle lines, keys, transfer requirements, and the work needed to move vulnerable people without turning rescue into abandonment. That competence can serve Judith, an evacuation, or a negotiated handover depending on what happens. Her allegiance, control, cooperation, route, custody decisions, transfers, survival, and role at the Hollow Feast remain live adventure state.

references.title: Corin Pike
references.summary: A fifteen-year-old Pike Mill apprentice used as Judith’s page, who knows the separated Mercy Book leaves, hidden page-number key, service routes, and coercive naming system from inside Blackbriar Hall.
references.content:
## An apprentice made into a route

Corin Pike is fifteen, nephew to Cora Pike of the mill household, and one of the seven children Judith’s naming system has marked. Blackbriar Hall calls him an apprentice and uses him as a page. He carries separated Mercy Book leaves between the petition hall, study, servants’ passage, and Underhall so that no one servant holds the whole household account.

## The numbers beneath the bed

Corin copied the page numbers and hid them under his bed slats. He also marked routes Captain Cleft could not easily watch. That knowledge can reconnect scattered entries, expose which leaves are missing, and make the house’s service geometry legible without treating the boy as a key adults may spend.

## A person before a component

A written name can compel Corin or open reflected paths through what he carries, but coercion does not erase his observations, kinship, or agency. This sheet cannot say where his body or vessel has gone, who holds either, or whether he will help. Establish his safety and willingness in the scene before treating his route knowledge as available.

references.title: Garran Pike
references.summary: Judith’s practiced roadkeeper and prisoner-wagon driver, who knows every fixed landmark, hidden compartment, route key, and handoff joining Mercy House, Crow Wood, Blackbriar Hall, the White Pits, and the Underhall.
references.content:
## The man who keeps the roads

Garran Pike knows the weight of a concealed passenger, the sound of a drugged prisoner against floorboards, the lime that works into a wheel after a body run, and the difference between a false turn and a fixed grade. For years he has moved children, witnesses, confiscated goods, sealed orders, and unburied dead while telling himself that transport is not judgment.

## Olla walking beside the wagon

Judith keeps Garran obedient through Olla Pike, his wife, whose body the Worm in White can force along the orchard road. Garran knows that the thing standing under Olla’s ankle bell is not a restored wife. He nevertheless treats each delivery as payment for one more night in which her face remains visible. That grief explains the bargain; it does not absolve the locked compartments behind him.

## A road action proves a break

Garran’s stable competence includes the iron road key, crow handoffs, the prisoner road, Mercy track, orchard route, and service tunnel. None of that proves he still holds the wagon, papers, prisoners, or key. Track Olla and his allegiance where events place them; a change of heart counts only when it becomes a material road action.

references.title: Saint Mercy House
references.summary: Blackbriar’s effective charitable house and coercive custody institution, joining public care, hidden naming, transferred illness, records, dormitories, infirmary work, and routes to Judith’s wider household system.
references.content:
## Care that places a person inside an account

Saint Mercy House feeds children, treats patients, stores medicine, teaches lessons, and keeps winter beds. Its usefulness is not a disguise added after corruption. Judith made the care dependable because every admitted person also entered a room, form, obligation, or custody chain she could inventory. The House is therefore both a real institution and one of the mechanisms by which relief becomes ownership.

## Public rooms and hidden work

The petition hall, refectory, schoolroom, kitchens, visible dormitory, records room, punishment passage, mirror dormitory, suspended infirmary, east bridge, and transfer cabinet form one operating system. Residents know different pieces of it. The hidden naming rooms, symptom bottles, service passages, and transfer orders matter because they are joined to ordinary food, schooling, medical labor, and staff competence.

## Capacity is never automatic

The House can shelter, feed, treat, transfer, conceal, record, or harm only through actual people, beds, stores, bottles, keys, routes, and receiving households. Count those resources room by room when the company arrives. A place sheet supplies no free bed, loyal staff member, safe exit, accepted inspection, or receiving household.

references.title: Blackbriar Hall
references.summary: Judith Crowl’s public household government, where charity stores, petitions, seizures, accusation work, service routes, pact channels, and the descent to the Hollow Feast meet under one roof.
references.content:
## A house that governs by receiving

Blackbriar Hall is manor, relief office, court lobby, storehouse, and private household at once. Petitioners enter beneath gifts Judith has made visible; seized goods and charity stores pass through rooms where gratitude, title, and punishment are written beside one another. The house makes her claim feel domestic even when it is performing government.

## Twelve rooms and several roads

The thorn terrace, petition hall, charity stores, counting room, dining room, ash gallery, study, guest rooms, servants’ passage, warm cellar, thorn court, undercroft gate, and locked stair form the stable house. Public petition, formal inspection, service tunnel, reflected corridor, marked hearth, and direct assault reach different parts of that geometry and expose different carriers.

## Occupants remain unsettled

The Hall can hold records, stores, patients, staff, guards, prisoners, pages, prepared gifts, and pact apparatus without guaranteeing that any remain when reached. Its geometry opens routes and custody problems; it does not place Judith, open the Underhall, preserve a record, command a servant, or settle who receives the estate afterward.

references.title: The Burned Refuge
references.summary: The granary where Judith barred nineteen promised refugees inside and welcomed the Guest in Ash, leaving an outward-opening door, restored names, and a freely offered hearth as the material terms of repair.
references.content:
## A shelter made into a betrayal

During the famine, nineteen road people worked on Saint Vey’s refuge granary after Judith entered them on the refuge roll. On the third night she barred the outer doors, accepted the Guest in Ash across the threshold they trusted, and recorded every victim as safely discharged. The fire burned inward because the promised shelter itself had been turned against them.

## Doors, names, and a truthful fire

The stable site includes the barred west doors, surviving measures and household marks, the roll niche, loft, ash ring, and the false shelter ledger’s connection to the place. Repair has three distinct obligations: open the original doors outward, restore all nineteen names under free witness, and burn the lying ledger in a hearth freely offered by someone Judith betrayed.

## Ruin is not repair

Breaking a wall, burning the granary while barred, scattering unnamed ash, or using coerced fire repeats the wrong rather than completing the obligation. Measure repair in doors opened outward, people named under witness, the false ledger handled truthfully, ash controlled, and a hearth freely offered. The ruined granary grants none of those acts by itself.

references.title: The White Pits
references.summary: Judith’s orchard burial ground, where thirty-one plague dead were erased in quicklime and later bodies were added, joining false fees, transferred illness, unburied remains, and the Worm in White’s claim.
references.content:
## Bodies denied a final witness

The White Pits lie beneath Judith’s orchard: lime shed, founding trenches, renewal trench, old cart approach, and sunken bell post. During the pox, families paid for honest burial. Judith removed tags, laid thirty-one bodies in quicklime, denied each one a final witness, and used the missing account to welcome the Worm in White. Later victims and inconvenient patients entered a separate renewal trench.

## Identification before lifting

The founding dead retain household marks, fee fragments, objects, bodily distinctions, and surviving family records. Safe work requires names, separate labels, protective equipment, labor rotations, prepared transport, and a real destination before remains leave the lime. The honest bell states where the dead were found and who denied them; it does not replace careful identification or disposition.

## A site, not an automatic conclusion

The Pits preserve the founding betrayal and the material conditions needed to answer it. Count progress in protected workers, honest names, lifted remains, labeled transport, bell witness, and final disposition. The orchard’s existence supplies no labor, cart, audience, safe trench, or completed burial.

references.title: Chapel of the Free Witness
references.summary: Blackbriar’s deliberately open chapel, preserving the honest bell and divided threshold, burial, and naming offices that require free witnesses, material repair, and public responsibility.
references.content:
## A threshold that refuses hidden ownership

The Chapel of the Free Witness was built so that no patron, reeve, household, or priest could quietly convert another person’s dependence into title. Its open threshold, nave, bell beam, vestry records, three incomplete manuals, and undercroft preserve procedures rather than a sovereign answer. Judith closed it under a famine ordinance because public witness disrupted command and separated gifts from consent.

## Three offices kept apart

The threshold office tests household welcome and revocation. The burial office joins name, body, witness, and final disposition. The naming office distinguishes an owner’s identity, an unborrowed reflection, and the order in which a stolen name may safely return. The honest bell carries those acts into public hearing; clergy alone cannot complete them from memory.

## Openness exposes what enters

The chapel can reveal a token, stolen ash, written command, or uncovered vessel without neutralizing it automatically. Its threshold and surviving offices explain how work can be done; they do not reopen the building, repair or commission the bell, remove hidden tokens, assemble free witnesses, or make the roof a safe refuge.

references.title: Moonless Mere
references.summary: The black water where Judith lowers silvered names to the Child Behind Glass, preserving reed shore, vessel hooks, an unborrowed basin, drowned records, and reflected routes that depend on controlled identities.
references.content:
## Water that borrows a face

Moonless Mere is a reed-bound black pool with vessel hooks, an unborrowed basin, a standing reflection, and a drowned cabinet of older names. Judith brings written names here so the Child Behind Glass can lend voices, dreams, false recognition, command, and reflected passage. The water is a pact site and a route surface, not a mind that knows every traveler.

## An unborrowed reflection

A safe restoration establishes the owner through the person or a free witness, finds a reflection not supplied by the Child, speaks the name back, waits until the reflection belongs to its owner, and only then breaks the vessel. An absent person’s name can be protected and prepared without pretending their body, consent, or guardianship has been resolved.

## Reflections have endpoints

The Mere can join only corresponding uncovered surfaces and controlled names. Covering a mirror, separating the written name, or breaking the pact closes that route rather than rewriting geography. Read each body, vessel, witness, bargain, recovery, and destination from the current state; the water never promises that a name or person remains where first found.

references.title: Crow Wood
references.summary: A fixed woodland road exchange whose streams, ridge, culvert, burned boundary, tunnel, roosts, and carrier-dependent false turns connect Judith’s prisoners, messages, bodies, stores, and pact routes.
references.content:
## Difficult woodland, not a changing world

Crow Wood does not brood or rearrange itself. Saint Orra’s brook runs south, the white quarry ridge remains east, the Burned Refuge marks the western boundary, the orchard culvert leads toward the White Pits, and the root-cut tunnel reaches Blackbriar Hall. Wagon grade, stream flow, ruts, and fixed landmarks remain honest even when a traveler’s attention does not.

## A carrier makes the wrong road persuasive

Blackthorn, stolen ash, controlled names, Mercy custody papers, marked gifts, and guiding crows can make one junction seem familiar and another disappear from notice. Removing or isolating the carrier stops further redirection; it does not move the traveler back or erase the road already taken.

## Where channels exchange cargo

The prisoner road, familiar roosts, orchard track, Mercy track, service road, and refuge boundary let paper, ash, bodies, prisoners, stores, and reflected commands change hands. Start each visit by marking the actual wagon, messages, prisoners, crows, escorts, carriers, keys, and last witnessed destinations. The map fixes geography, not traffic or control.

references.title: Underhall of the Hollow Feast
references.summary: The chamber beneath Blackbriar Hall where sixty-three household doors, the Mercy lectern, token table, seven choir bays, dead settings, patron chairs, and Judith’s place assemble a valley-wide welcome.
references.content:
## An account book made architectural

The Underhall lies beneath Blackbriar Hall. A wagon gallery overlooks sixty-three household doors, a four-sided Mercy lectern, a blackthorn token table, seven choir bays, thirty-one founding settings with later places, three patron chairs, and Judith’s seat. The main stair, service tunnel, reflected routes, and valid hearth crossings enter different parts of the chamber.

## Two of three make the common welcome

The Hollow Feast joins three components: written hosts in the Mercy Book, physical household carriers in the token network, and at least four controlled living voices in the captive choir. The valley-wide welcome operates while any two remain joined. Judith’s place coordinates them but is not itself a component. A surviving pact gives the Unwelcome Court a patron through which to inherit the assembled claim.

## Earlier work changes the room

Public revocation turns doors outward. Returned names silence bays. Honest burial removes settings and bodily protection. The opened Refuge distorts the Guest’s thresholds. At arrival, count the actual doors, pages, sockets, voices, bodies, lieutenants, patrons, and feast stage. No sheet preloads those results or decides Judith’s position and the chamber’s resolution.

references.title: The Blackthorn Men
references.summary: Judith’s distributed guard and transport force, divided between willing officers, marked bodies subject to visible command, and ordinary paid retainers who remain capable of refusal.
references.content:
## One badge, several kinds of service

The Blackthorn Men guard executions, records, roads, wagons, institutions, and Blackbriar Hall under Captain Varro Cleft. Some serve willingly for wages, status, fear, or advantage. Others carry written names, cure receipts, tokens, coins, lodging oaths, or stolen ash through which Judith can seize bodily control. The company is therefore neither an innocent enchanted mass nor a body of equally free actors.

## Command leaves a sign

A mark heats, a jaw locks, eyes gray, a tongue bleeds, feet turn, or a borrowed voice emerges before forced movement. Removing the carrier, hiding the full written name, sounding the honest bell against a false closure, or receiving a lawful release may break one command. None of those acts excuses willing cruelty performed before or after compulsion.

## Force must still travel

Blackthorn reach depends on actual guards, officers, messages, wagons, keys, roads, and a place willing or unable to receive them. A badge identifies a coercive chain, not the order currently in force. Place the real roster, marks, prisoners, casualties, refusals, and route control where the latest witnessed action left them.

references.title: The Unwelcome Court
references.summary: The otherworldly court Judith sought through three deliberate betrayals, able to inherit a valley-wide household invitation only through surviving patron claims and at least two joined feast components.
references.content:
## Three guests, not one hidden master

The Unwelcome Court is the relation among the Guest in Ash, the Worm in White, and the Child Behind Glass. Judith did not discover it by accident. She chose one betrayal for each patron and later built relief, custody, burial, household, and record systems around the access purchased. The Court is not a fourth pact that restores a broken chair or replaces a patron whose obligation has been completed.

## A common invitation must be assembled

The Court can enter Blackbriar Vale as one household only when Judith’s Hollow Feast joins at least two of three components—the Mercy Book, token network, and captive choir—and at least one patron claim remains capable of inheriting the welcome. Smaller household claims may survive after the valley-wide rite fails, but they do not become the same common invitation by rhetoric alone.

## No automatic midnight

Time gives Judith pressure, not omnipotence. The Court requires actual pages, carriers, living voices, doors, bodies, routes, and a surviving violation. Its three patrons may still exist while the common invitation fails. Read manifestation, inheritance, household exposure, and final outcome from the feast actually assembled.

references.title: The Guest in Ash
references.summary: The patron welcomed through nineteen refugees barred inside a promised granary, granting carrier-bound hearth passage, inward fire, threshold denial, and soot concealment while enforcing plainly accepted invitations.
references.content:
## Welcome betrayed at the door

Judith’s first pact began when she promised nineteen road people shelter, barred Saint Vey’s granary from outside, and welcomed the Guest in Ash across the trusted threshold. The Guest’s claim is not fire in general. It is shelter deliberately converted into confinement and an account that says the betrayed were safely received.

## An offer must be accepted

The Guest can offer warmth, passage, concealment, a dead guide, or safety from another channel. Questions, silence, threats, and “not now” do not accept. Taking the offered coal, saying “come in,” deliberately crossing a door the Guest creates, or otherwise agreeing to the stated exchange gives it a path through that person’s next accepted shelter. Existing marked hearths and stolen ash provide finite carriers; they do not make every flame Judith’s door.

## Repair the obligation, not the scenery

Open the original granary doors outward, restore all nineteen names under witness, and burn the false shelter ledger in a freely offered hearth belonging to someone Judith betrayed. Judge progress from those material acts and from bargains knowingly accepted in play. The patron sheet does not make an offer accepted, place a carrier, weaken a threshold, or sever the pact.

references.title: The Worm in White
references.summary: The patron welcomed through thirty-one plague dead erased in quicklime, able to move sickness, animate abandoned flesh, spoil stores, and place Judith’s wounds on the unburied.
references.content:
## A tally made from unreturned bodies

Families paid Judith to carry thirty-one plague dead to honest ground. She removed their tags, laid them in quicklime beneath the orchard, and denied each body a final witness. The Worm in White entered through that missing account. Later bodies and patients could renew or exploit the channel without becoming the founding betrayal themselves.

## Harm travels through a prepared line

The Worm can move illness between labeled bodies, animate abandoned remains, spoil stores, return a purchased cure, and shift Judith’s injuries onto the unburied. It acts through bodies, white roots, bottles, wounds, burial omissions, and prepared routes. A body still moving is not thereby restored, and a transferred symptom does not identify who consented to bear it.

## The dead require an honest disposition

Identify the founding thirty-one, lift them safely from quicklime, state where they were found and who denied them, and give each honest burial or controlled burning beneath the honest bell. Partial identifications and lifted bodies are real progress. Count patients, bottles, workers, transfers, manifestations, and final dispositions where the operation actually leaves them.

references.title: The Child Behind Glass
references.summary: The patron served through stolen written names lowered into Moonless Mere, lending borrowed voices, dreams, false recognition, written command, reflected roads, and the Glass Nurse.
references.content:
## A price Judith returned to pay again

The Child Behind Glass named its price before Judith paid it. She copied children’s chosen names onto silvered slips, sealed them behind mirrors, and lowered the names through Moonless Mere. Saint Mercy House then turned intake, dormitory, transfer, and record work into a steady acquisition system. The Child’s apparent youth does not make the bargain innocent or accidental.

## A name opens a bounded surface

The Child lends voices, dreams, false recognition, written commands, reflected routes, and the composite Glass Nurse. Those acts require a controlled name and an uncovered corresponding surface. A vessel can support command at a distance, but it is not the owner’s body, consent, testimony, or living voice. Covering glass blocks one surface; it does not return the stolen name.

## Identity must return before glass breaks

Establish the owner through the person or a free witness, use an unborrowed reflection, speak the name back, wait for the reflection to belong to its owner, then break the vessel. A hook or written name identifies possible leverage, not the owner’s body, route, consent, restoration, or safety. Track each separately.

references.title: The Mercy Book
references.summary: Judith’s distributed household account, whose master index joins separated pages of gifts, signatures, custody, and accepted obligations into the written-host component of the Hollow Feast.
references.content:
## Mercy entered as title

The Mercy Book records households through the aid Judith claims they accepted: food, fuel, cure, burial, bed, custody, protection, or place. Its fraud is not that every entry invents the benefit. It treats the benefit as permanent authority over names, rooms, heirs, thresholds, and dependents.

## One book carried in pieces

The master index joins separated leaves carried among Saint Mercy House, Blackbriar Hall, servants, and the Underhall. Each leaf contains only a few households so no ordinary carrier holds the complete plan. Signatures and entries become the written-host component only when pages and index are materially joined at the Mercy lectern.

## Evidence and machinery must be separated

The Book can be removed from its lectern, divided from its index, corrected under free witness, rendered unusable after evidence is copied, or destroyed after stolen names and necessary records are separated. Burning joined pages while the Guest remains active can send signed ash toward household hearths. Treat every page, index, signature, carrier, correction, and destruction as material state rather than assuming the component is assembled.

references.title: Blackthorn Tokens
references.summary: Physical household and command carriers—tokens, splinters, coins, marked gifts, cure receipts, oaths, and stolen ash—through which Judith can identify a claimed door, redirect a bearer, or seize a marked body.
references.content:
## A claim needs something that can be carried

Judith’s blackthorn system uses carved tokens, splinters, coins, marked lamps, cure receipts, lodging oaths, stolen hearth ash, and comparable accepted gifts. A carrier may identify a household door, support a marked road, warm near a claimed threshold, or give written command access to a particular body. The objects differ; none is a universal license over everyone nearby.

## Heat is evidence, not consent

A token warming, bleeding soot, burning the skin, or pulling attention reveals an active connection. It does not prove that the present resident accepted the gift, that the bearer remains willing, or that a reeve may answer for a whole household. A resident may revoke their own welcome and remove, cool, cover, isolate, or publicly surrender the carrier.

## The network must match real households

At the Hollow Feast, token echoes matter only while the table can match them to actual household carriers and written hosts. Warmth proves a connection, not ownership or consent. Record the owner, bearer, revocation, command, household exposure, and socket separately; the network survives only where those carriers still meet the written account.

references.title: The Honest Bell
references.summary: The Chapel of the Free Witness’s repairable portable bell, which makes concealed transfers visible and gives bodies, wounds, names, and public refusals a shared audible witness without completing their obligations automatically.
references.content:
## A bell closed under the wrong law

The honest bell belonged to the Chapel of the Free Witness until Judith used a famine ordinance to close the chapel and divide its fittings. Its beam, clapper, metal, fastening, and surviving records can be reunited into a portable instrument. The bell’s authority comes from free public witness and accurate use, not sacred rank or possession alone.

## What the sound reveals

At the White Pits, the bell states where the dead were found and who denied them. Near transferred illness, it makes white movement visible. Against commands resting on the false chapel closure, it can release a marked body. At the Underhall, it lets wounds and the dead answer under their own names rather than Judith’s feast response.

## Sound does not finish the work

The bell does not identify a body without evidence, provide a burial place, return a name, supply labor, or make a witness free. A repairable bell is not yet repaired, commissioned, present, or audible. Record its parts, carrier, location, audience, sounding, effect, and survival each time the company relies on it.

references.title: Silvered Name Vessels
references.summary: Folded written names sealed behind narrow mirrors, allowing the Child Behind Glass to coordinate identity, command, and reflected passage while remaining distinct from each owner’s body and living voice.
references.content:
## A written name behind borrowed silver

A name vessel is a folded slip bearing a chosen name, sealed between a mirror’s backing and glass. Judith’s current system uses seven narrow vessels around a central mirror that combines their reflections into the Glass Nurse. The object can carry identity and command across distance; it is never the same thing as the person whose name it holds.

## Cover before carrying

Safe handling begins with dull unpatterned cloth. Do not read the name aloud in a reflected room. Keep the vessel with a free carrier, record the owner separately, and preserve it for an absent person rather than declaring that person rescued. Covering prevents observation and reflected coordination but does not heal the owner or restore the name.

## Return before breaking

Use the owner or a free witness to establish identity, find an unborrowed reflection, speak the name back, wait for the reflection to belong to the owner, and only then break the vessel. The safe sequence is stable; every vessel’s owner, location, covering, condition, witness, restoration, injury, and final disposition must be established separately.

encounters.title: Saint Orra's Gallows
encounters.summary: Judith places Mara's torch in Tomas's hands, making an illegal execution a public receipt for obedience.
encounters.opening_view: First-light rain has blackened Saint Orra's green. Mara Sedge names her missing daughter from the pyre while her eleven-year-old son grips an unlit torch. Brother Caldus holds a death roll whose cut edge has been rebound; Reeve Pell hides a blackthorn token beneath his coat. Judith Crowl waits under a dry black umbrella. “Tomas,” she says, “a good son proves his innocence by burning the witch who bore him.” One guard lowers her spear. Captain Cleft says, “Three.”
encounters.content:
## The immediate wrong

Mara Sedge has been condemned without a lawful witness. Her thirteen-year-old daughter Nell vanished from the family croft three nights ago. Mara named Judith Crowl as the taker. Before the hour turned, Judith had produced a blackthorn poppet from Mara's chimney, supplied an emergency ordinance, and given Reeve Ansel Pell the courage to sign what she had already decided.

Now Judith has placed the torch in the hands of Mara's eleven-year-old son, Tomas. If he lights the pyre, she promises to receive him and seven-year-old Pate into Saint Mercy House instead of examining them as a witch's accomplices. The bargain kills more than Mara. It makes Tomas carry the act, teaches Pate what refusal costs, and gives the crowd a child whose obedience can be called consent.

## Why the commission reaches the pyre

Ysra's original writ predates Mara's arrest. Duplicate burial fees, missing graves, and two returned Mercy House letters had already caused the canon to send examiners into the vale. After Nell vanished and Mara named Judith, Brother Caldus sent a short addendum by a parish rider who met the commission before dawn. Judith's crow route intercepted enough of the first writ to know the expected day of arrival, but not which road the examiners would use. She therefore denied Mara the customary answer-night and moved the burning to first light. Their arrival before Tomas raises the torch is the consequence of two competing courier networks, not chance.

The commission reaches the green under the original inspection writ and Caldus's addendum. The seal neither dismisses the reeve nor commands his guards; it demands the docket, names witnesses, preserves evidence, and holds Mara alive while the charge is reviewed. Judith expected scrutiny after the ash cooled. She did not expect a rider to put the examiners on the correct road before dawn.
## The execution clock

Run the opening in visible steps rather than resolving it with one check.

1. **The oath.** Beadle Odo Vane reads the charge and makes the crowd repeat that every household “receives mercy and its mistress.”
2. **The torch.** Captain Varro Cleft gives Tomas the torch. Tomas does not move until Judith names Pate.
3. **The challenge.** Present the commission, accuse Judith, question the process, interfere physically, address the crowd, or pretend to cooperate.
4. **The first order.** Judith tells Pell to proceed, orders a marked guard to seize one examiner, or offers a public bargain.
5. **The break.** If resistance holds for even a few moments, Mara or Brother Caldus can put a concrete irregularity before the crowd. Judith must then retreat, escalate openly, or risk losing her appearance of lawful calm.

Questions do not shorten the count. Judith wants witnesses to see Tomas obey, so she leaves enough silence for the boy's choice to become public—and enough time for the examiners to act.

## The legal fault

The emergency conviction fails Blackbriar's own parish custom in four ways:

- no sworn accuser names an act they personally witnessed;
- the poppet was produced by Judith rather than found by the reeve or parish clerk;
- Mara was denied the customary night to answer a capital charge;
- no record explains why Nell Sedge is absent or who holds custody of her.

Canon Ysra's seal authorizes a temporary stay while those defects are examined. Pell knows this. Odo Vane insists that famine ordinances let the reeve ignore it; the cited ordinance concerns spoiled grain, not witchcraft. Put the docket in Caldus's hands and he can expose the substitution before the crowd.

## The commission and later authority

The writ permits four things at the opening: inspect parish and charitable records, preserve evidence, suspend this execution while defects are reviewed, and protect named witnesses from immediate seizure. It does not transfer civil rule, command every guard, authorize unrestricted searches, or make the commission owner of Judith's stores and estate.

Practical authority may broaden only when the fiction supplies a new basis. A discovered unlawful detention supports immediate rescue. A household may invite protection and revoke its own carriers. Pell may issue limited guard-release, evidence-preservation, or evacuation orders in public. Caldus and chapel witnesses may commission the bell and counter-rites. Violence by Judith's people supports ordinary defense and detention. None of those bases authorizes permanent government, secret punishment, or final disposition of property and children. Record which person or institution accepts responsibility for every expansion.

## People on the green

- **Mara Sedge** is burned, exhausted, and exact. She names children, dates, remedies, and the point at which an officer's story changes. She will not ask Judith for mercy. “My Nell is thirteen. She was taken on the ninth night after first frost. Put that in your book before you call her gone.”
- **Tomas Sedge** is eleven and has no patience for an adult's moral summary. He wants to know where Pate is, whether Mara can breathe, and who will stop Cleft if he drops the torch. Give him one credible adult action and he acts at once.
- **Judith Crowl** speaks at household volume. She uses debts as surnames—“Ansel whom I restored,” “Caldus whose sister I housed,” “Tomas whom I am still willing to forgive”—and leaves silence after each one so the crowd must either accept the account or break it aloud.
- **Reeve Ansel Pell** hides decisions inside passive grammar: the charge “was brought,” the ordinance “was found,” the child “has been asked.” Judith cured his wasting sickness by moving it into Elian Darr, and Pell signed the first seizure order afterward. He wants a lawful reason to stop. He also wants someone else to be the person who stopped.
- **Brother Caldus Merrow** remembers missing pages by date, ink, and burial fee. Judith threatened his widowed sister Adela and her son Lark until he concealed discrepancies. Under protection, he can name the substituted leaves and the day the Chapel of the Free Witness was closed.
- **Beadle Odo Vane** prefers offices to people: accused, dependent, household, beneficiary. He drafted the emergency charge knowing the famine ordinance did not authorize it. His daughter received a Mercy House place, and he has chosen repeated cruelty to preserve that advantage.
- **Captain Varro Cleft** speaks in distances and commands. He enjoys the moment when a lawful phrase gives him permission to hurt someone. If Judith leaves, he is the person most likely to continue the burning because the crowd has already been arranged for it.
- **The marked guards**—Edrin Bale, Samet Kett, Will Noll, and Piers Vey—carry tokens or signed cure receipts. Written names can force their bodies, but command arrives visibly: teeth lock, eyes gray, and the mark heats before movement.
- **The unmarked guards**, Cora Pike and Hen Joss, are paid retainers rather than enthralled servants. They can refuse Cleft once the commission is public and the crowd stops lending silence.

## The crowd is not one thing

Use four visible groups.

- **Sedge patients** remember births Mara attended without payment. They will not begin a fight, but two will cut ropes or carry Mara if someone else breaks the first line.
- **Mercy households** owe Judith food, medicine, fuel, or custody. Some defend her sincerely because the aid was real. They become uncertain when asked whether aid authorized Tomas's punishment.
- **The prosecuted families** stand at the edges: Darr, Rusk, Mett, Vey, and Fen households. They possess fragments of older cases and are watching to see whether any challenger survives public speech.
- **Judith's dependents** include paid servants, token-bearing patients, and people with children in Saint Mercy House. They repeat her accusations quickly because they fear what silence will cost.

A crowd response should follow a witnessed act. One villager speaking does not create a mob; one villager speaking and remaining protected makes a second speaker possible.

## Evidence present on the green

The green yields evidence before anyone leaves.

- Mara can direct them to the packets beneath her floor and accuse Saint Mercy House.
- The trial docket shows the false ordinance and Blackbriar Hall as recipient of seized property.
- Caldus can name the old chapel bell and the burial discrepancy.
- The poppet uses Blackbriar petition paper, though the clove-waxed thread is easier to identify at the croft.
- Pell's blackthorn token warms when Judith crosses the courthouse threshold without a spoken invitation.
- Judith's retreat through hearth ash leaves inward-bending flame and warm soot.
- Quill and the other crows depart toward Crow Wood carrying red prisoner-wagon cloth.
- A commanded guard continues speaking in Judith's voice after she has crossed the green.

Award observed facts immediately. Their implications can wait until someone investigates them.

## Ways to stop the burning

### Invoke the commission

Reading the seal aloud and naming one procedural defect forces Pell to acknowledge a stay unless Judith openly overrules him. Mara then needs a custodian and a protected destination. Pell's gaol leaves her within reach of the reeve's token.

### Separate Tomas from the torch

A character can reach Tomas, block Cleft, soak or seize the torch, or give the boy a believable place for Pate and Mara. Tomas is not a test of persuasion skill; he is a child being threatened. Remove the immediate threat or accept the danger of rescuing him physically.

### Turn the process against Judith

Questioning Caldus, examining the poppet, or forcing Odo to cite the ordinance can expose a lie before the whole green. Judith answers with a counteraccusation and an offer: surrender Mara to Saint Mercy House and the burning stops. Acceptance saves Mara now but places her inside Judith's strongest institution.

### Use force

Violence can rescue Mara. Distinguish Judith, Cleft, the four commanded guards, the two ordinary guards, and the crowd. Initiative grants Judith no free massacre. If she loses the green, she retreats through ash and sends retainers after the rescuers.

## Failure forward

If the execution stops only at a cost, choose the smallest consequence that follows.

- Tomas drops the torch after the pyre catches, leaving Mara burned and in urgent need of care.
- Cleft wounds or arrests one rescuer while Mara is cut free by someone else.
- Pell grants a stay but orders Mara confined in an unsafe location.
- Judith escapes with the poppet or docket while Mara is carried clear.
- The crowd accepts Judith's accusation that the examiners endangered children, making Saint Mercy House harder to inspect openly.
- Mara dies only after a meaningful chance to reach her. Her directions survive through Tomas, Caldus, and the croft, but the village loses its strongest living accuser.

## Public result

Record the strongest witnessed refusal, not a numerical morale score.

- **Silence broken:** someone publicly contradicts Judith and survives the scene.
- **Authority contested:** Pell recognizes the stay, a guard refuses Cleft, or the false ordinance is exposed.
- **A witness protected:** Mara, Tomas, Caldus, or another speaker leaves under credible protection.
- **A household commits:** a named household offers food, shelter, transport, testimony, or public revocation.

These commitments determine what villagers will risk later. Judith may punish a person or break a refuge, but she cannot make the crowd forget that resistance occurred.

## Judith's first retaliation

Once the stay is invoked or Mara is removed from the pyre, Judith sends Odo the altered Renewal schedule and commits the feast clock. That ordinary order starts preparations below Blackbriar Hall; it does not grant her an extra remote attack. She then chooses one response supported by a channel she still possesses.

1. She names the examiners as paid witch-finders who manufacture guilt for coin and has Odo post the accusation.
2. She orders Saint Mercy House sealed because outsiders have threatened the children.
3. She sends Quill and three hearthlings to the Sedge Croft to destroy Mara's notes and seize Tomas.
4. She transfers Pell's old sickness back into him and blames the stay.
5. She commands one marked guard to accuse the examiners of bewitchment while the guard's unmarked comrades watch the possession begin.

Every retaliation reveals method. Judith turns dependency, gratitude, or duty into evidence against the victim.

## Leaving the green

Possible departures include Mara under temporary ecclesiastical custody, Tomas as a protected witness, the reeve's records in examiner hands, or flight after a violent rescue. Name every vulnerable person's destination, escort, food, care, and any token, name, gift, or hearth ash Judith owns there.

Unless she is physically restrained, Judith leaves the green for Blackbriar Hall by carriage after the public break. If she instead uses a hearth or reflected route, show the valid carrier, name the destination, and move her one body there. Do not place her at Saint Mercy House and Blackbriar Hall at the same time.

Whatever the route, the village has seen someone refuse Judith publicly. Fear remains, but her claim that resistance is impossible has been broken once.

## Route branches from the green

The opening does not prescribe a visit to the Croft before every other response. Once the immediate burning is resolved, five actionable branches are visible.

- **Sedge Croft:** Mara, Tomas, Quill's flight, the clove-waxed poppet, and the stolen hearth ash point toward the family evidence and refuge problem.
- **Saint Mercy House:** Nell's disappearance, Judith's custody threat, and the promise made to Tomas point directly toward the children and dependent residents.
- **Blackbriar Hall:** the trial docket names the estate as recipient of seized property, and Judith's own departure or servants provide a route for direct confrontation.
- **Chapel of the Free Witness:** Caldus, the false ordinance, and the burial discrepancy point toward the closed parish protections and truthful bell.
- **Crow Wood:** Quill, the red prisoner-wagon cloth, and marked guards point toward the moving captive and familiar network.

Record the first destination, every vulnerable person sent elsewhere, and Judith's last confirmed physical location. One chosen branch gives her time to spend a surviving channel against another. The unchosen encounters remain occupied and active.
